newsitem.title: CHINA: Christopher says Wang's jailing no block to summit.
newsitem.headline: Christopher says Wang's jailing no block to summit.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Tuesday the jailing of prominent dissident Wang Dan will not be an impediment to U.S.-China summits.

The comment, as he arrived for his first visit to Beijing since a disastrous 1994 trip, was the clearest signal yet that the Clinton administration has downgraded human rights as it seeks to mend frayed ties with China and press a broad agenda.

Christopher also said that in talks with President Jiang Zemin and other leaders on Wednesday he would urge China to halt nuclear cooperation with Iran and to persuade North Korea to maintain a freeze on its nuclear programme.

This would include asking China to cancel a deal to provide Iran, which Washington considers a state sponsor of terrorism, with a uranium conversion faciity that could help Tehran produce fuel for nuclear bombs, officials said.
"I expect I'll be discussing human rights and the rule of law issues at all of my meetings," Christopher told reporters en route from Sapporo, Japan, where he spent the night.

"With respect to the meetings at the highest levels, I'd emphasise the importance of the overall relationship, the fact that we need to have a steady and comprehensive approach to the relationship, that's not rooted in a single issue," he said.
The United States and China have already announced plans to hold a series of high-level meetings, including Christopher's trip and an exchange of summits in their respective capitals.
President Bill Clinton and Jiang could announce a timetable when they meet in Manila on Sunday at an economic summit.

Christopher's remarks reflect an evolution in U.S. policy toward China over the last two years and his refusal to risk a furore over human rights ahead of meetings Wednesday with Jiang, Premier Li Peng and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

After Clinton took office in 1992, China's human rights record was tied to U.S. trade privileges. But when ties deteriorated with disputes over rights, trade, Taiwan and arms sales, Clinton dropped the link and pursued progress on a broad agenda, not focused on one issue.

U.S. officials acknowledge the awkwardness of holding summits when Beijing has cracked down sharply on dissidents. But they say the other approach did not work and China is such a key power that comprehensive engagement is the only option.
Wang, a leader of the 1989 Tiananmen Square pro-democracy demonstrations, was jailed after a military crackdown on the protestors. He was released in 1993 after world appeals.
Now he has been imprisoned for 11 more years on charges of subversion. A Chinese court rejected his appeal last Friday.
Coming before Christopher's visit, the action was seen as another Beijing warning on human rights. But some officials say the action is more related to Chinese domestic politics.
Christopher did not criticise the Wang verdict, although his spokesman earlier expressed U.S. disappointment over it.
Just before Christopher arrived in Beijing in 1994, his top human rights adviser held talks with prominent dissident Wei Jingsheng, who was arrested as he left the meeting.
Christopher then suggested cancelling his trip. Wei was released before Christopher landed in Beijing, but the incident inflamed a tense situation and ruined Christopher's trip.
On this trip, Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck, the top human rights aide, is not meeting any pro-democracy activists while with Christopher in Beijing.

On China's nuclear cooperation with Iran, Christopher said that due to Tehran's record on terrorism, attempts to acquire arms of mass destruction and opposition to Mideast peace, "I simply think Iran is not to be trusted with this highly sensitive technology."
U.S. officials say China plans to sell Tehran a uranium conversion facility.

North Korea, meanwhile, has threatened to break a 1994 accord with the United States under which Pyongyang froze its nuclear programme in return for $4.5 billion in new nuclear power reactors and alternative energy supplies.
The threat came after South Korea delayed sending technicians to the North to do preparation work for the reactors.

Christopher said he would urge China to use its influence with North Korea to maintain the freeze. He said he would also urge South Korea, whose foreign minister he meets in Manila later this week, to honour its commitments under the deal.
